tagline.text: A Manila maritime history museum where you can walk aboard a full-scale galleon

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Seaside Boulevard and Sunset Avenue, SM Mall of Asia Complex, Bay City, Pasay

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (indoor visit, open year-round)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱675–1,500 (admission plus a meal, per adult)

children.text: This maritime history museum opened in May 2026 in the SM Mall of Asia complex, close to Manila Bay. Inside its dome stands a full-scale replica of the 17th-century galleon Espíritu Santo, with decks and cabins you can walk through. It tells the story of the galleon trade linking Manila and Acapulco and of Philippine seafaring culture in one place.

Museo del Galeón is a maritime history museum inside the SM Mall of Asia (MOA) complex in Pasay, at the corner of Seaside Boulevard and Sunset Avenue. The area is famous for its Manila Bay sunsets, so it fits easily into a day of shopping and strolling. The building is a four-storey dome with about
of exhibition space. The SM Group provided a lot of about 5,000 sqm; the idea dates to 2010, construction began in November 2014, and after long delays the museum opened to the public on
The centerpiece is a full-scale replica of the 17th-century galleon Espíritu Santo. It is about
long and

high and stands in the middle of the dome, so its size is the first thing that strikes you at the entrance. The original ship was built in 1603 with forced labor and sailed the trade route between Manila and Acapulco, Mexico. The replica is made mostly of fiberglass and similar materials, and visitors can climb on deck and explore the cannon-lined interior, the crew quarters and the captain's cabin.

From 1565 to 1815, about 250 years, the galleon trade was the first regular sea trade to link Asia, the Americas and Europe. Chinese silk and porcelain were exchanged for silver in Manila and shipped to Mexico, while crops such as squash, corn, tomatoes and cacao traveled the other way into Asia. The museum tells this story from a Philippine point of view. Following the narrative from prehistoric times, when Filipinos already sailed in boats such as the balangay, through the Magellan expedition to the galleon era, you come to understand why Manila was a hub of world trade.

Please check the current status before you go. At opening, two of the four galleries were open first and the rest were reported to be in preparation; some reports said galleries III and IV would open in October 2026, but whether they have opened could not be confirmed. Before visiting, check the official website or social media to see which areas are open. In the early days there was also an announcement that visitors who bought a ticket early could return after the remaining galleries opened, so check the latest notice on that too.
This is the museum's signature attraction. A galleon about

long has been built to scale, and you can walk the main deck, the open-air upper deck, the cannon-lined interior and the crew quarters. The captain's cabin has a table once used for plotting courses, so you can feel like a navigator.

A replica of the balangay, the traditional boat Filipinos sailed long before the Spanish arrived, greets you near the entrance. Compared with the Spanish galleon, it shows at a glance two cultures that sailed the same seas in different ways.

blocks.title: Ancient Mariners and Their Sea Routes

children.text: The first gallery, "Ancient Mariners and Their Sea Routes," covers Philippine seafaring before colonization. Maps, timelines, explanatory panels and artifacts show how the people of Southeast Asian islands built trading networks.

The second gallery, "Circling the World and Back," tells how the Magellan expedition reached the Philippines. Figures such as Lapulapu and Rajah Humabon appear, and statues of Lapulapu and Maniago stand on the third floor.

A large LED display wrapped around the inside of the dome shows calm seas, storms and constellations in the night sky. Lighting and sound blend with the ship to create the feel of being on deck at dusk, though the interior is rather dark.

blocks.title: Fleet of the Centuries and Pillars of Exchange

children.text: Around the dome is the "Fleet of the Centuries," showing 181 galleons from different eras, and ten "Pillars of Exchange" hold artifacts. Chinese blue-and-white porcelain, maps and exchanged crops show concretely what the galleon trade meant.

The second floor introduces Chinese blue-and-white porcelain and the crops that moved in the Columbian Exchange, such as squash, corn, tomatoes, cacao and spices. It is a corner that makes you think about where the food on Philippine tables came from.

The third floor displays Spanish-era religious art, including a wooden carving of the Virgin Mary and a 17th-century polychrome wooden tabernacle. You can see how the Catholic culture that arrived on the galleon trade took root in the Philippines.

Head toward Seaside Boulevard, enter the museum and check your ticket. Start by admiring the balangay replica at the entrance.

Board the Espíritu Santo and explore the deck, the cannon-lined interior and the captain's cabin. The interior is dark, so watch your step.
Leave the museum and stroll the Manila Bay promenade while you wait for the sunset. The sea breeze is cool around sundown.

items.title: From the MOA mall to the museum

children.text: The museum is connected to SM Mall of Asia. Exit the mall toward Seaside Boulevard and take the escalator near the Tong Yang restaurant to reach the second-floor entrance.
If you drive, use the North Parking building or the lot on Seaside Boulevard; spaces fill up quickly on weekends.
Most exhibits are indoors, so weather rarely forces you to give up the visit. The November–May dry season is best if you also want to enjoy the walk to the museum and a Manila Bay stroll.
The museum is open Wednesday to Sunday and closed on Monday and Tuesday. Weekends and holidays bring many families, so a quiet weekday morning is recommended.

Because the museum is inside the MOA complex, meals are very easy to arrange. The mall has a food hall, fast food, Korean restaurants and cafes. Early visitor accounts mentioned a Mexican restaurant on Level 3 of the North Entertainment Wing, a restaurant in the food hall, one on Seaside Boulevard and a chocolate cafe on Level 2 of MOA Square. Menus and prices change, so check on site.

For lodging, hotels around the MOA complex and in Bay City, Pasay are convenient. Being close to the airport, they suit a stay the night before departure or right after arrival, combining the museum with the sunset. Hotel rates vary a lot by date, so compare them yourself on a booking site.
Check and buy tickets in advance on the official website (museodelgaleon.org) or the museum's official channels to cut waiting time on site.
Ticket sales end at
, one hour before closing, so hurry if you come in the late afternoon.
According to early information, visitors with a ticket for the galleries that opened first can return once the remaining galleries open. Keep your ticket and check the latest notice.
The interior of the ship is dimly lit. Wear light shoes and hold children's hands.
Reading the panels takes time. Allow at least
2 hours
Read a little about the galleon trade and Magellan before you go and the exhibits become far more interesting. For children, describe it as a ship-exploring game.
After the museum, adding a sunset at the MOA bayside promenade makes the day more complete.
The museum is closed Monday and Tuesday, so check the day of the week in your plan first.
In its early days some galleries may not be open yet, and prices and hours may change. Be sure to check the official notice before you visit.
The museum is closed on Monday and Tuesday. Holidays may have separate hours.
The inside of the ship and its stairs are dark and sloped, so watch your step. Ask staff on site which areas are accessible with a stroller or wheelchair.
Traffic around MOA is very heavy on weekend afternoons and long holidays. Waits for a Grab can be long.
Photography and bag rules are set by the museum, so follow the instructions at entry.
Keep valuables on you and watch your belongings in the mall crowds.
A large shopping mall directly connected to the museum. Its restaurants and facilities make it a convenient place to eat and rest before or after your visit.
You can see the Manila Bay sunset from the MOA promenade. It is close to the museum and within walking distance.
A marine-themed attraction in central Manila; travel time varies greatly with traffic. It pairs well if you have children.
The Spanish colonial walled city was the departure port of the galleon trade. Going after the museum keeps the historical context connected.
